ff-1024-paycheque-trail.caption:
Payday. Where should the money go first? 🇨🇦 A simple order a lot of planners use:

1. A safety net: one month of bills in savings, then build toward 3 to 6 months.
2. If your employer matches retirement savings, put in enough to get the full match. It's free money.
3. Then invest in your TFSA, in a low-fee index fund, and leave it alone.

Why this order: the safety net stops a surprise bill from landing on a credit card. The match is an instant return. Then time does the rest.

Do this: this payday, set up one automatic transfer to stop 1. Add the others as you go.

Not guaranteed. Returns vary. Education, not advice.

ff-reel-1025-tfsa-withdrawal-trap.caption:
Putting TFSA money back? Wait. Here's the trap.

You take out $5,000 in March and put it back in June. Feels harmless. But the room from a withdrawal only comes back on January 1 of the next year. If you had no other room left, that $5,000 is an over-contribution, and the CRA charges 1% a month on it until it's out: $50 a month, about $350 from June to December.

Do this: before you put money back, check your room in CRA My Account (it shows your room as of January 1). Moving money between banks? Ask for a direct transfer, which doesn't count as a withdrawal.

Already did it? Take the extra out as soon as you can, and look up form RC243 (the TFSA return) on canada.ca.

The rule to remember: out this year? Back in January.

Send this to your TFSA friend.

Follow for one money move a day, in plain words.

ff-richhabits-01.caption:
Paid Friday. Broke by Wednesday? The habit: pay yourself first.

Rich Habits, Decoded No. 1. Each episode takes one money habit and shows you how to do it on a normal paycheque.

WHAT IT MEANS: savings come out the day your pay lands, automatically, before you can spend it. You live on what's left, instead of saving what's left.

WHY IT WORKS: you don't rely on willpower. In the 'Save More Tomorrow' study, workers who signed up to save automatically, with the rate rising at each raise, went from saving 3.5% of pay to 13.6% in about 3.5 years.

HOW TO DO IT (10 minutes in your banking app):
1. Open a separate savings account (ideally one that pays interest and that you don't see every day).
2. Set an automatic transfer for payday. Start at 10%; if that's too much, start at 1% or 2%.
3. Every raise: add 1 percentage point.
4. Leave it. The point is not having to decide again.

THE CATCH: if you carry card debt at 20%+, point the automatic payment at that first. Keep a small buffer so the transfer never bounces.

Do this: set one automatic transfer for your next payday, even if it's $10.

Rich Habits, Decoded No. 2 is Wednesday at 5 pm.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money move a day, in plain words.

lf-1023-resp-catch-up.caption:
No RESP yet? It's not too late. Here's the catch-up plan.

SOUND FAMILIAR? "We'll start next year." Then the baby is five.

THE PART NOBODY TELLS YOU: your child's grant room builds up every year from birth, even if you never opened an RESP. The government matches 20% of what you save through the Canada Education Savings Grant.

YOU PUT IN, THEY ADD (per year):
• $1,000 in → $200 added
• $2,500 in → $500 added (the normal yearly max)
• $5,000 in → $1,000 added (*only if you have unused room from past years)

Catching up, the grant can be up to $1,000 a year, until the full $7,200 per child is used.

CAN'T DO $5,000? $2,500 a year still gets the full $500, and any amount gets 20% added.

THE DEADLINE: grants stop at the end of the year your child turns 17. At 16 and 17 they only qualify if at least $2,000 went in before the end of the year they turned 15, or $100 a year in any 4 earlier years. So for an older child, start now.

Do this: this week, ask your bank to open an RESP and use your catch-up room. Bring your child's SIN.

The rule that stays: the room waits for you, but not forever.

Tonight at 7: how much you can still get, by your child's age.

lf-1024-roadmap-bedtime.caption:
Bedtime battle again tonight? Take the calm route 👉 5 stops, same order, every night.

🌙 Lights down, same time every night.
🛁 A warm, calm bath.
🪥 Teeth, pyjamas, screens off.
📖 Read together: your lap, their pick. This is the bonding stop. The same book 10 times is fine.
💤 Cuddle, a song, the same goodnight words, lights out.

Why it works: in a study of more than 10,000 mothers in 14 countries, young children with a bedtime routine every night fell asleep faster, woke less at night and slept more than an hour longer than children who never had one. The more nights a week, the better. The American Academy of Pediatrics sums it up as Brush, Book, Bed.

Do this: tonight, pick your 5 stops and do them in the same order. Same time tomorrow.

Send this to the parent who's still up at 9:30 negotiating.

General information only, not medical advice.

#bedtimeroutine #toddlersleep #bonding #parenting #canadianparents

lf-reel-1025am-crying-peak.caption:
Worried you're spoiling your baby? "Don't pick her up, you'll spoil her." You've heard it. It's not true.

THE SCIENCE: the American Academy of Pediatrics says you cannot spoil a young baby with attention, and that if you answer their calls for help, they'll cry less overall. Responding quickly in the first few months is the best way to handle crying.

THE TIMELINE (NHS): crying often starts building around 2 weeks, peaks around 6 to 8 weeks, then slowly eases. It's a normal stage, not a sign you're doing it wrong.

YOUR CALM-DOWN KIT (check fed, changed, warm first):
• Rock: in a chair, or sway in your arms.
• Sing or talk: the same song every time.
• Walk: in your arms or the stroller.
• Steady soft sounds, gentle back pats, a burp, a warm bath.
Try one at a time for a few minutes before switching.

If the cry sounds different from usual, or baby seems unwell (fever, not feeding, floppy), call your doctor or your health line (811 in most provinces).

WEEK 2 → WEEK 8 → MONTH 3: the build, the peak, the ease. Every time you pick them up on the way through, baby learns the world answers.

Do this: next cry, check fed, changed, warm. Then rock and sing, the same song every time.

The rule that stays: pick them up. You can't spoil a newborn.

lf-1025-follow-crying.caption:
Baby won't stop crying? Start here: pick the line that fits and follow it 👉

🍼 Last feed a while ago? Offer a feed. Hunger is often the reason.
🧷 Fed, but still fussing? Check the diaper, and whether they're too hot or too cold.
🤗 Fed, dry, still crying? Hold them close and sway, sing, or go for a walk with the stroller.

If baby seems unwell (fever, not feeding) or the cry doesn't sound like their usual cry, call your doctor or your health line. And if it's all too much, put baby down safely on their back in the crib and step away for a few minutes. That's OK.

Do this: save your health line in your phone now: 811 in most provinces (Manitoba: Health Links, 1-888-315-9257).

lf-1025-hold-million-words.caption:
One book a day: 296,660 words from books by age 5. Hold the dots and slide 👀

📕 Never read to: about 4,662 words.
📗 1–2 books a week: 63,570.
📘 3–5 a week: 169,520.

That's from researchers at Ohio State, who counted the words in the most-borrowed board books and picture books at their library.

Why it matters: the words in books are words kids may not hear in everyday talk, and reading is also 10 calm minutes on your lap, with your full attention. That's bonding and brain-building at the same time.

lf-reel-1025-step-away.caption:
Tried everything, still crying, and you're at your limit? That happens to loving parents too. Here's the plan.

THE NHS ICON ADVICE: crying is normal, comfort can help, and it's OK to walk away if you've checked baby is safe and the crying is getting to you. Never, ever shake a baby: shaking can cause serious brain injury.

THE 10-MINUTE RESET:
1. Put baby on their back in their crib or bassinet, with nothing else in it.
2. Close the door and go to another room for a set time, like 10 minutes.
3. Breathe out slowly. Make a tea. Text your person: "Can you come?" or "Can you talk?"
4. Go back, check baby, and start again calmer.

If baby seems unwell, or the cry sounds different from usual, call your doctor or your health line (811 in most provinces). In an emergency, call 911.

AND FOR YOU: if the crying leaves you feeling hopeless for weeks, tell your doctor or midwife. That's part of postpartum care too.

Do this: tonight, pick your step-away person (partner, friend, sister) and tell them they're it.

The rule that stays: safe crib, closed door, ten minutes.

How long do you stay on one screen before switching? In 2004 it was about 2.5 minutes. Guess first 👀

Why it matters: every switch costs a little focus, and 47-second hops add up to a day that felt busy but didn't get far.

Do this: for your next task, go full screen. One window, nothing else, until it's done.

lh-reel-1025am-planning-fallacy.caption:
Why does everything take longer than you think? You're not bad at planning. Everyone is.

THE STUDY: students guessed their thesis would take 34 days on average. It took 56. Even their worst-case guess, 49 days, was too short. Only about 3 in 10 finished in the time they predicted. It's called the planning fallacy.

WHY IT HAPPENS: when we plan, we picture the day where everything goes right: no sick kid, no slow reply, no file that won't open. And we quietly ignore how long the last one actually took.

THE FIRST FIX:
1. Before you guess, ask "how long did this take LAST time?", not "how long should it take?"
2. Look it up if you can: your calendar, old emails, the last report's date.
3. Then add half again. Think 2 hours? Plan 3. Think a week? Plan a week and a half.

WHAT CHANGES: Day 1, your plan looks worse on paper. Week 1, you finish when you said you would, maybe for the first time in a while. Month 1, people start trusting your "by Friday".

The rule that stays: plan from your past, not your hopes.

Do this: today, add half again to your next time guess.

lh-reel-1025-unpack.caption:
"It'll take an hour." It won't. Here's the fix that's backed by research.

THE RESEARCH: in a study, people who listed every step of a task before guessing how long it would take made longer, more realistic guesses. Hidden steps are where the time goes. It works best for tasks with lots of parts.

HOW TO DO IT ("update the website", unpacked):
1. Find the old photos (15 min)
2. Wait for the new ones from Sam (1 day of waiting, 5 min of asking)
3. Write the new text (45 min)
4. Send it for a check, then fix the comments (30 min + a day)
5. Upload and test on your phone (20 min)
"An hour" was really about 2 hours of work and 2 days of waiting.

THE HIDDEN STEPS TO ALWAYS ADD: waiting for someone, setup (logins, finding files), the back-and-forth, travel, and the check at the end.

WITH THIS MORNING'S FIX: compare your total with how long it took last time, and if they disagree, trust last time.

WHAT CHANGES: Day 1, Monday's plan fits inside Monday. Week 1, fewer 9 pm "how is this not done?" moments. Month 1, your estimates become the ones people plan around.

The rule that stays: guess the steps, not the task.

Do this: tonight, take Monday's biggest task, write down its steps, then guess the time.

lh-1025-climb-one-percent.caption:
1% better a day = 38x in a year. Climb it 👉

Day 73: 2.1x. Day 146: 4.3x. Day 219: 8.8x. Day 292: 18.3x. Day 365: 38x.

That's the famous maths in James Clear's Atomic Habits: 1.01 multiplied by itself 365 times is about 37.8. And the flip side: 0.99 to the 365th is about 0.03. Tiny daily habits decide which way you go.

Why the climb looks slow, then steep: improvements build on improvements, like compound interest. At 1% a day, you roughly double every 10 weeks, so the early weeks feel like nothing. That's the base everything else stands on.

Real life is lumpier than maths, and nobody improves by exactly 1% a day. The lesson stays: small gains, repeated, stack.

Do this: pick one habit. Tomorrow, do it 1% better: one more page, one more minute, one less tab.

lh-oneword-01.caption:
Inbox open all day again? Today's word: Batch.

One Word No. 1. Each episode is one word that guards your focus.

THE RESEARCH: in a 2-week study, people who checked email only 3 times a day felt less stressed than when they could check as often as they liked.

HOW TO BATCH:
1. Pick 3 times: say 9:30, 1:00 and 4:30.
2. Close the email tab (and turn off email notifications) between them.
3. At each check: reply, file or schedule. Nothing stays "unread to deal with later".
4. Worried about missing something urgent? Tell people to call or text for urgent things.

THE CATCH: if your job is answering email (support, dispatch), batch something else, like chat or news.

Do this: tomorrow, write your 3 check times on a sticky note and close the tab.
